name: Packaging Corporation of America
moat_justification: Scale, vertical integration and a dense plant network give a real freight / service cost edge in a bulky, low value-to-weight product, and a historically disciplined low-cost operating culture — but containerboard is a commodity, pricing follows industry supply/demand rather than company-specific pricing power, and larger rivals can match scale.
fragility_flags: STALE_FY: latest fiscal year ended 9 months ago — check TTM/quarterly OE and consider --base-oe-ps override
NI_OCF_DIVERGENCE: net income and operating cash flow differ by >40% in 2023, 2025 — find the one-off (tax deposits, impairments, WC swings) before trusting the OE base
WIDE_SCENARIO_SPREAD: super-bull IV is 4.5x super-bear IV — uncertainty is huge; confidence should not be high
HIGH_NET_DEBT: net debt is 4.9x normalized OE — levered OE can vanish fast; stress the bear cases
one_liner: Quality integrated containerboard producer, moat 5/10 — does not clear 15% at $232.58 (weighted IRR 6.78%, weighted IV@15% $76.42); it would need a price near $76.42 to clear 15% on the weighted case.
moat_for: Vertical integration — mills feed its own corrugated plants, insulating volume from the open containerboard market
Scale as the third-largest North American containerboard producer, enlarged by the Greif mills and plants
Dense corrugated plant network close to customers — freight is a major delivered cost for bulky boxes
Proven through-cycle profitability — OE positive 5 of the last 5 fiscal years
moat_against: Commodity product — containerboard / box pricing is industry supply/demand driven, no durable pricing power
Larger, equally integrated rivals can match scale and capacity
Uncontrolled input costs — recycled fiber (OCC), freight, energy and chemicals squeezed Q2 2026 margins
Cyclical end demand and industry capacity additions can pressure prices for years
